articles.summary: Ben Shelton will face Alexander Zverev in the 2026 U.S. Open final. Here's how to tune in.
articles.body:
American tennis star Ben Shelton will face Alexander Zverev in the 2026 U.S. Open men's final. This will be No. 8 seed Shelton's first grand slam final, but he'll be facing this year's French Open winner and top seed. The last time an American man took the U.S. Open title was in 2003, when Andy Roddick defeated Spain's Juan Carlos Ferrero. As it currently stands, Zverev is a career 5-0 against Shelton , with only one set dropped.

The 2026 U.S. Open men's championship final is this Sunday, start time still TBA. The Shelton vs. Zverev final will air on ABC and stream on the ESPN Unlimited app. Here's everything you need to know to watch the men's championship final at the 2026 U.S. Open tennis tournament .

Streaming: ESPN Unlimited, YouTube TV, DirecTV and more

Ben Shelton vs. Alexander Zverev match time:

The ESPN suite of channels will cover the entirety of the 2026 U.S. Open. The Ben Shelton vs. Alexander Zverev match will air live on ABC and ESPN Deportes.

ESPN Unlimited subscribers will be able to stream the entirety of the U.S. Open, too.

articles.title: How Aryna Sabalenka built a business empire beyond tennis with $50.4 million in career prize money and major brand deals
articles.summary: International Sports News: Aryna Sabalenka has turned her rise to the top of women’s tennis into a growing business platform built around prize money, major sponsorships, media .
articles.body: Aryna Sabalenka has turned her rise to the top of women’s tennis into a growing business platform built around prize money, major sponsorships, media visibility and investments. The Belarusian star has earned $50,422,999 in career WTA prize money according to the latest WTA records, while Forbes estimates that she earned $36.1 million in the 12 months covered by its 2026 highest-paid tennis players list, including $13.1 million on court and $23 million off court. Her commercial portfolio now includes global names such as Nike, Wilson, Gucci, Audemars Piguet, Emirates and Whoop, while she has also put money into businesses including OneOff and WTGL. Her business growth has not come from simply attaching her name to products. Sabalenka has increasingly used her personality, audience and success to build a brand that can earn money even when she is not playing a tournament.How did Aryna Sabalenka build the financial foundation for her business empire?Sabalenka’s tennis career remains the biggest foundation of her financial success. Her prize money has grown sharply alongside her results at Grand Slam tournaments and WTA events.The latest WTA records list her career prize money at $50,422,999, making her one of the highest-earning women in tennis history. She has also won 24 WTA singles titles, including four Grand Slam championships.Her biggest breakthrough came at the 2023 Australian Open, where she won her first Grand Slam singles title. She successfully defended that title in 2024 before winning the US Open in 2024 and 2025.The 2025 season was especially important for her finances. Sabalenka won four singles titles, finished the year as world No. 1 and set a WTA single-season prize-money record of $15,008,519.Her career financial growth can be seen through these figures:Financial milestoneAmountCareer WTA prize money$50,422,9992025 WTA single-season prize money$15,008,519Forbes 2025 total earnings$30 millionForbes 2025 on-court earnings$15 millionForbes 2025 off-court earnings$15 millionForbes 2026 total earnings$36.1 millionForbes 2026 on-court earnings$13.1 millionForbes 2026 off-court earnings$23 millionForbes’ 2026 figure is particularly important because it shows how much Sabalenka’s business side has grown. Her estimated off-court earnings rose to $23 million, compared with $15 million in the previous Forbes female-athlete ranking. Forbes’ methodology includes sponsorships, appearance fees, licensing and certain business returns, but does not deduct taxes or agents’ fees.That means her tennis results are not just producing prize money. They are increasing the value of her name to companies.Which sponsorships have helped Aryna Sabalenka expand her brand?Sabalenka has built a wide sponsorship portfolio covering sports, luxury, technology, travel, fashion and consumer products.Forbes currently lists Anheuser-Busch InBev, Audemars Piguet, Emirates, Fanatics, Gucci, Master & Dynamic, Nike, Whoop and Wilson Sporting Goods among her sponsors. Forbes also reported that she added several new partnerships in 2026, including Emirates, Material Good and Stella Artois.Her partnerships cover different parts of the market:Nike: sportswear and footwear.Wilson: tennis equipment.Audemars Piguet: luxury watches.Gucci: fashion and luxury.Whoop: fitness and performance technology.Emirates: international travel.Fanatics: sports merchandise.Master & Dynamic: premium audio.Anheuser-Busch InBev: beverage brands.Stella Artois: a newer 2026 commercial partnership.Material Good: jewelry.Electrolit: sports drinks.IM8: nutrition and supplements.Sabalenka’s sponsorship strategy has become more varied as her fame has grown. Instead of relying only on traditional tennis companies, she is working with luxury, lifestyle and consumer brands.Forbes reported that she had added partnerships with six brands in 2026, showing how quickly her commercial portfolio has expanded.Her personality is also a major part of the strategy. Sabalenka has openly said that she wants partnerships to fit who she is rather than simply accepting every available deal. In a Forbes interview, she described authenticity, personality and emotional connection with fans as important parts of her brand.This gives companies more than a famous tennis player. They get an athlete with a recognizable personality who can create content and connect with fans.How has Aryna Sabalenka moved from endorsements into investments?The next stage of Sabalenka’s business growth has been investing in companies rather than only promoting them.That difference is important. A sponsorship generally pays an athlete for promotional work, while an equity investment can give the athlete a financial interest in a business. However, the exact size of Sabalenka’s stakes and the amounts she has invested are not publicly available for every company.Forbes has reported Sabalenka’s involvement with consumer and wellness businesses, while its 2026 coverage also identified newer investments.Her publicly reported investment interests include:CompanySectorReported connectionBeekeeper’s NaturalsWellnessInvestorOlipopFunctional beveragesInvestorIM8SupplementsEquity stake/investment reportedOneOffAI fashion discoveryInvestorWTGLWomen’s golfInvestorForbes previously identified Sabalenka as an investor in Beekeeper’s Naturals and Olipop. In August 2026, Forbes reported that she had also put capital into OneOff, an AI-powered fashion discovery platform, and WTGL, a new women’s golf league.Sabalenka has also been linked to IM8, a nutritional supplement brand. Forbes reported in 2025 that she had taken an equity stake in the company.These investments show that her business interests are moving beyond tennis.There is a clear pattern in the companies connected to Sabalenka:Wellness and nutrition.Functional beverages.Sports and fitness.Women’s sports.Fashion technology.These areas also fit naturally with her identity as a professional athlete. That makes the investments easier to connect with her existing audience.At the same time, there is no reliable public evidence that Sabalenka owns a large collection of companies or operates a traditional corporate empire. The available evidence points to a growing portfolio of partnerships and selected investments rather than a large company she personally founded and runs.How is Aryna Sabalenka turning her personality and tennis success into a long-term business?Sabalenka’s final piece of the business strategy is her personal brand. Her commercial value is no longer based only on how many tournaments she wins.Her move from IMG to Evolve, the sports agency founded by Naomi Osaka and Stuart Duguid, was reported by Tennis.com as part of her greater control over her business affairs. Tennis.com also reported that her estimated 2025 earnings reached about $30 million, with approximately $15 million coming from prize money and another $15 million from off-court income.That increased control has helped her develop a broader identity away from tennis.Sabalenka has become known for showing more of her personality through social media and interviews. She has talked about wanting fans to see her life outside competition, including cooking, shopping, packing and makeup.This matters commercially because her value does not disappear when a tournament ends.Her long-term business strategy can be summed up in four areas:Tennis success: Grand Slam wins and the world No. 1 ranking create global attention.Sponsorships: Major brands turn that attention into direct commercial income.Investments: Equity stakes give her exposure to businesses beyond endorsement payments.Personal brand: Social media and media appearances help her maintain visibility throughout the year.Her 2026 earnings show how effective that model has become. Forbes estimates her total earnings at $36.1 million, including $23 million off court. That means off-court income represented the larger part of her estimated earnings for the period.The numbers also show why calling Sabalenka a growing businesswoman is more accurate than simply calling her a highly paid tennis player. Her career prize money has passed $50 million, while her commercial income is now measured in tens of millions of dollars annually.Sabalenka’s business empire is still developing, but the direction is clear. She has used her tennis success to build relationships with global brands, expanded into luxury and lifestyle categories, and started investing in businesses that operate outside professional tennis. With $36.1 million in estimated 2026 earnings and $23 million coming from off-court sources, her commercial career is becoming almost as important to her financial profile as her performance on the court.The key point, however, is that her exact net worth remains unknown. Public figures show her earnings, prize money, sponsorships and reported investments, but they do not reveal her taxes, expenses, agent fees, private assets or the value of her individual investments. Therefore, the strongest description is that Aryna Sabalenka has built a multimillion-dollar athlete brand and an expanding investment portfolio, rather than a traditional business empire made up of companies she owns outright.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: US Open 2026 results: GB's Neal Skupski and Christian Harrison wins men's doubles title
articles.summary: Britain's Neal Skupski and American partner Christian Harrison win the US Open men's doubles to secure their second Grand Slam title together.
articles.body:
Britain's Neal Skupski and American partner Christian Harrison won the US Open men's doubles title to claim their second Grand Slam trophy together.

The fifth seeds did not drop a set in New York as they beat sixth seeds Tim Puetz and Kevin Krawietz 6-4 7-6 (8-6) to secure the title.

Victory adds to Skupski and Harrison's Australian Open triumph in January in what was their first Grand Slam as a pairing.

Skupski had suffered a heartbreaking defeat in last year's US Open final, missing three championship points when he reached the showpiece alongside fellow Briton Joe Salisbury.

He and Dutchman Wesley Koolhof were also beaten in the 2022 final.

Salisbury later took a break from tennis because of anxiety, which led to Skupski partnering up with Harrison.

Cheered by the Flushing Meadows crowd, who rallied behind home hope Harrison, the pair saved a set point in the second set tie-break before Skupski sealed victory with a smash at the net.

"I don't know what to say really, I'm still in shock. The speech gets a little bit easier once you've won," said Skupski.

"Losing twice and having championship points in the final last year was a tough part of my career, but it's amazing what a year does in tennis."

Skupski and Harrison secured the first and only break of the match in the first set, the American slamming a backhand winner down the line to lead 4-3 before seeing out the opener.

The second set remained on serve until the tie-break, where Puetz and Krawietz profited from a return which clipped the net and wrong-footed Harrison to give the Germans a set point.

Skupski and Harrison saved it and then brought up championship point as the noise levels rose on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

Skupski dropped to his knees in celebration after sealing victory before turning to hug Harrison.

Victory at Flushing Meadows marks Skupski's third doubles Grand Slam title after he won at Wimbledon in 2023 alongside Koolhof.

Skupski also has two mixed doubles Grand Slam titles to his name after winning Wimbledon in 2021 and 2022 with American Desirae Krawczyk.

articles.title: $100 chicken nuggets? $38 sandwiches? What astronomical US Open food prices say about the future of sports fandom in America
articles.summary: The US Open — like so many other high-level concerts and sporting events — has now become a social media laboratory, one whose value is not in experiencing,...
articles.body:
NEW YORK — I was halfway through my third caviar-topped chicken nugget when two simultaneous thoughts occurred to me: First, this is a very good nugget, but not $100 good. Second, this is the kind of thing that spawns revolutions … and not the kind that end well for the caviar-topped nugget eaters.

This year, the US Open achieved its true destiny, leveling up from mere tennis tournament to full-on influencer festival with tennis backdrop. Maybe it's the photoshoots or Tiktok dance routines interrupting actual play, maybe it's the long-shot prayer of finding reasonably priced tickets, or maybe it's the brisk sale of three-figure fast food, but the US Open has taken American sports to a new level. Hope you've been saving up for that bucket-list experience .

As the crowds flowed into the Billie Jean King Tennis Center on Saturday for some of the final matches of the 2026 US Open, some sought out seats around one of the many tennis courts in the complex. Others headed straight for the merch stores to snag some prized gear. And many, so so many, went straight to one of the Grey Goose stands in search of the US Open's most prized treasure: the beloved Honey Deuce.

A Honey Deuce — Grey Goose vodka, lemonade, raspberry liqueur and three honeydew melon balls, served over ice in a commemorative cup — is the most notable of the US Open's many food and beverage options, but other, far more expensive offerings are coming for its crown.

So, with that in mind, I decided to embark on an expense-account-wrecking challenge: the $200 US Open lunch. Let's just see how the 1 percent dines, shall we?

Honey Deuce ($23): Journalists aren't supposed to drink on the job, so I'll just say that a "good friend of mine" purchased this one and enjoyed it very much, though a significant portion of that enjoyment came from the fact the Honey Deuce was served over ice on a very warm day. Chilled gasoline with a honeydew melon garnish would've tasted pretty good on Saturday. And yes, my "friend" immediately sent a pic of the glass to his text chain. It's the law at the US Open.

Salt Hank's French Dip Sandwich ($38): This is the white-hot food offering at this year's US Open, so much so that Salt Hank's has been given the prestigious end slot among all the food stalls, the better to accommodate the wraparound lines. I was the third person in line at 10:50 a.m., and by the time Salt Hank's started taking orders at 11, at least 40 people were already behind me. As for the sandwich — "dry-aged prime rib, provolone, caramelized onions, horseradish aioli, baguette" — it was a damn good sandwich. Seriously, one of the best I've ever had. And even so, it was overpriced by half. But I will dream of that sandwich in the years to come. Oh yes, I will.

US Open Souvenir Cup ($12.50): It's a cup. A pretty cup, yes, but still — a cup. Good for backyard barbecues where you can casually mention, "Oh, I got this when I was up at the US Open. Maybe one day you can go, too." (You will not be invited to backyard barbecues after this.)

The Golden Set at COQODAQ ($100, not a misprint): The nuggets are delicious, yes, light and golden-fried. But they're not really the selling point here, nor is the crème fraîche, the diced chives or the pickled radish. No, you're paying for the 30 grams — just over an ounce — of Tsar Imperial Daurenki caviar from Petrossian, which adds a rich, complex finish to the chicken nugget. A whole lot more than honey mustard does, anyway.

Honeycomb Fudge Slam at Van Leeuwen ($10.75 & up): Ice cream dealers were early adopters of the mega-expensive snack treat trend, so they're perfectly at ease charging you exorbitant rates for cones that would be three bucks at the beach. This US Open-only flavor is indeed delicious, though on top of French Dip, caviar, chicken and (possibly) other beverages, it hit my gut like an Aryna Sabalenka serve. This is my fault, not the Honeycomb Fudge's.

Total cost: $184.25. For one person. For lunch. That's … a lot.

This is all part of a trend that's consuming the elite levels of American sports: The death of the cheap seat , and everything that goes with it. American sporting institutions have become extremely skilled at extracting the maximum possible revenue out of every single ticketholder. If a four-figure ticket price is a little too rich for your blood, well, step aside, friend, there's someone who'll happily pay.

You can't really blame the US Open for fishing where the whales are. The sport has always enjoyed a refined, white-napkin, strawberries-and-cream veneer. Prestige comes with a cost; if everyone could afford it, what's the point?

Thing is, as exorbitant as these prices are, there are people — lots of people — out there willing to pay them. A cashier at COQODAQ estimated they were selling 250 of the $100 Golden Sets each day, and just one of the dozens of Honey Deuce servers estimated they alone were pouring 1,500 of the pink-and-melon drinks a day.

Now, it's worth noting that nobody in their right mind is purchasing chicken nuggets with caviar at a tennis tournament just because they're hungry. (There are, indeed, plenty of lower-cost food offerings.) The entire reason to drop a Benjamin on nuggets is so that you can show other people you can, in fact, drop a Benjamin on nuggets. (It's me, hi. I'm the problem.) Everyone here who's taking a selfie holding up a Honey Deuce has to maneuver around the five other people who are also taking selfies with their Honey Deuces.

And that's the entire issue here, that the US Open — like so many other high-level concerts and sporting events — has now become a social media laboratory, one whose value is not in experiencing, but in sharing the experience.

The same fate befell the Masters last year, when hype surrounding the legendary golf tournament's merch, particularly the highly coveted limited-edition gnomes , boiled over. Influencers walked through the gates, waited in line at the merch building for well over an hour, bagged mid-four-figures' worth of Masters-branded goods, then left to film their haul for adoring viewers — with absolutely zero interest in the golf that's supposed to be the centerpiece of the event.

Rumors persist that Augusta National will stop selling the gnome next year in order to return some of the sanctity to the tournament. Augusta National, the only locale in America that enforces a mass cell phone ban, can get away with that. Nobody else can.

That, really, is the only answer to this madly spiraling inflation of sports costs — a willingness to forgo short-term cash grabs in favor of long-term goodwill. (And that's assuming that the people with the power to set prices want to "answer" this at all.) Just for perspective's sake: At the Masters, you can buy 66 pimento cheese sandwiches for the cost of one US Open Golden Set, or almost four beers for the cost of one Honey Deuce.

This economic pain tolerance is the new reality of sports fandom in America. If you're willing to pay, the elite leagues, tournaments and races will happily take your money. And if you're not, well, you can find chicken nuggets almost as good as the US Open ones at any decent drive-thru. Trust me on that.

articles.title: Rybakina se lleva todo el botín de Nueva York y deja a Sabalenka sin nada
articles.standfirst: La kazaja, que el miércoles le quitó el número 1 a la bielorrusa, le gana la final del US Open tres días después
articles.summary: La kazaja, que el miércoles le quitó el número 1 a la bielorrusa, le gana la final del US Open tres días después
articles.body: A principios de semana, Aryna Sabalenka confesaba que el número 1 de la WTA le daba igual si se coronaba por tercera vez consecutiva en el cuadro individual femenino del US Open. Elena Rybakina, su gran rival, la ha dejado sin nada. La kazaja será este lunes la nueva número uno mundial —lo es virtualmente desde el pasado miércoles— y esta misma derrotó el sábado a Sabalenka en la lucha por el título, por 6-4, 5-7 y 6-2, en 2 horas y 21 minutos. Ganó con clase, con un servicio directo. Lejos quedan las dudas físicas por culpa de una lesión en el talón que le hicieron ser duda en el certamen hasta última hora. Las finales de Grand Slam están para ganarlas más que jugarlas. Y acabar con esa misión le está costando un mundo a Aryna recientemente. La pasada campaña, hincó la rodilla en la última ronda del Open de Australia y Roland Garros. Y el pasado mes de enero, perdió la de Australia frente a Rybakina. La kazaja ya es un dolor de muelas para la tenista de Minsk, que no puede con su sangre fría. Se demostró en Melbourne y ha vuelto a pasar en Nueva York. Mientras Sabalenka es todo temperamento, a su repetida verdugo parece que todo le da igual. Aunque en el fondo no sea así. Recuperado su entrenador, Stefano Vuzkov, que hace dos años fue sancionado por la WTA por maltrato a la tenista, Elena responde con éxitos a la inversión millonaria del magnate, Bulat Utemuratov. El presidente de la federación kazaja de tenis estuvo detrás de la nacionalización de Rybakina en 2017. Cabe recordar que es natural de Moscú. Con una fortuna estimada de 3.700 millones de dólares, Utemuratov vibró como uno más en uno de los palcos de la Arthur Ashe neoyorquina. Rybakina es una máquina de precisión. No es de colgantes ni de tatuajes. A pesar de pegarle fuerte a la pelota son contados sus errores no forzados. Y es precisamente esa estadística la diferencia con Sabalenka. La bielorrusa acumula un fallo tras otro cuando entra en barrena. Le pasó en el quinto juego de la final y acabó entregando su servicio. Le costó la manga inicial. No llegaba al 40 por ciento de puntos ganados con el primer servicio. Aryna odia correr de un lado a otro y era exactamente eso a lo que le obligaban. Tuvo que cambiar de táctica y buscar los puntos en la red. A las palancas de la mejor tenista del planeta le ayudan su 1,84 metros. Sabalenka tiró de orgullo para fabricarse dos pelotas de segundo set. Era en el décimo juego del segundo set, con 15-40. Falló pero volvió a la carga en el decimosegundo asalto. Tanta insistencia tuvo premio y firmó las tablas en el marcador, que era lo que querían los aficionados que habían pagado la entrada. La más barata estaba en 500 dólares. A la bielorrusa le sobraban ganas, pero le faltaban piernas y le dolía la espalda. Encajó el segundo 'break' nada más empezar el tercer set y ya no tuvo margen para una segunda remontada. La flamante campeona del Abierto de los Estados Unidos se sitúa con una renta de 2.026 puntos respecto a Sabalenka. La próxima aparición de la kazaja será el día 23 de septiembre en Shenzhen con motivo de los cuartos de la Billie Jean King Cup que le va a enfrentar a la España de Carla Suárez.

articles.summary: El torneo reparte la mayor bolsa en premios para el campeón, que asciende a 5.500.000 dólares
articles.body: El US Open anunció un récord en premios para 2026, que ascendía a 108 millones de dólares. De esa cantidad, 11 corresponden a los campeones individuales en categoría masculina y femenina. Elena Rybakina, vencedora en féminas destronando a Aryna Sabalenka, se ha llevado a casa un talón de 5.500.000 dólares. Este es el mayor botín que jamás se ha repartido en la historia del tenis profesional. Su víctima, campeona de las dos últimas ediciones del Abierto de los Estados Unidos se conforma con 2.800.000 dólares.

articles.title: Elena Rybakina Beats Aryna Sabalenka to Win 2026 US Open Women's Final Bracket
articles.summary: Elena Rybakina is a first-time U.S. Open champion.
articles.body:
Elena Rybakina is a first-time U.S. Open champion.

Rybakina claimed a 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 win over two-time reigning champion Aryna Sabalenka to claim the women's singles title Saturday in Queens.

Rybakina, who clinched the world No. 1 ranking in the quarterfinals, started out her first U.S. Open final strong as her backhand made the difference in the first set.

Sabalenka fought back by slamming down a putaway shot to gain a 6-5 lead in the second set.

She sent the match to a decisive frame when Rybakina ended the set by shanking a forehand into the net.

Rybakina and Sabalenka each went into the third set having won 71 total points.

Sabalenka took the first game of the decisive set before Rybakina responded by rattling off two holds and a break.

Rybakina ultimately played a drama-free final set before closing out the win with her 12th ace of the match.

Sabalenka, a five-time major winner, was playing in her fourth straight U.S. Open final. She lost the 2023 tournament to Coco Gauff before winning consecutive titles over Jessica Pegula and Amanda Anisimova.

The loss drops Sabalenka's overall record in Grand Slam finals to 4-5.

Rybakina is now a three-time major winner. She won her second Grand Slam title by defeating Sabalenka in the Australian Open final earlier this year.

articles.title: Elena Rybakina dethrones Aryna Sabalenka to win her first U.S. Open title
articles.summary: Elena Rybakina won her first U.S.
articles.body: Elena Rybakina won her first U.S. Open title and punctuated her climb to the top of women’s tennis by beating Aryna Sabalenka 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 on Saturday. Rybakina had already been guaranteed to replace Sabalenka at No. 1 in the rankings next week and for good measure took the U.S. Open title that Sabalenka had won the previous two years. “It’s tough to find words right now, honestly,” Rybakina said. “I don’t expect nothing like this coming to this tournament. I’ve been dealing with a little bit with an injury, but somehow everything aligned together on my side.” It was the third Grand Slam title for Rybakina and the second this year — both against Sabalenka on hard courts. She opened the season by beating Sabalenka for the Australian Open title. This time, she stopped Sabalenka’s 19-match winning streak at the U.S. Open, where she hadn’t lost since falling to Coco Gauff in the 2023 final. “I really felt like home here and cannot wait to come back next year,” Sabalenka said. “I wish I could perform a little bit better but I guess next year.” Rybakina earned $5.5 million, the largest prize in Grand Slam history, and tied Sabalenka and French Open winner Mirra Andreeva with a tour-high three titles this season. Sabalenka took home $2.8 million but it was clear how little that meant to her, as she smashed her racket after a brief hug with Rybakina at the net. Sabalenka was trying to become the first person since Serena Williams from 2012-14 to win three in a row at Flushing Meadows. Rybakina dethroned the champ without even having her best stuff. The WTA Tour leader in aces got less than half of her first serves in but instead put Sabalenka under constant pressure with a strong return game, racking up 12 break chances and converting three, which was all she needed. The third meeting of No. 1 vs. No. 2 in a U.S. Open women’s final since 2000 was the first to go the way of the challenger. Williams was the top seed for the other two, beating her sister Venus in 2002 and Victoria Azarenka in 2013. The numbers didn’t signify much this time, because they are going to flip Monday. Sabalenka has held the top spot for 99 consecutive weeks, but Rybakina gained enough points to unseat her simply by reaching the semifinals. She didn’t stop there. The 27-year-old who was born in Russia but represents Kazakhstan won her first major title at Wimbledon in 2022 and now needs just the French Open to complete the career Grand Slam. And it’s clear her power — and her ability to absorb her opponent’s — was something that unnerved Sabalenka. A native of Belarus, Sabalenka sometimes swings from her heels, like a golfer trying to unleash a 300-yard drive, grunting “Aaaaahhhh!” as she takes her mighty cuts. Rybakina’s power comes more easily. There is little sound coming from her side of the net besides the squeaking of her sneakers, and she rarely shows any hint of stress. “I think Elena is probably — not nonchalant, I don’t want to say that, because she’s not nonchalant — but just no reaction ever,” Gauff said after losing to Rybakina in the semifinals. Rybakina did show some frustration after pulling a backhand wide with a break point in the opening game of the third set, but soon she had taken charge of the match for good. Sabalenka had won the two other meetings this season, on the hard courts at Indian Wells and Miami, and leads their rivalry 10-8. But her season then took a strange dip after those victories. Sabalenka fell to Naomi Osaka in the fourth round at Wimbledon, then returned to action with consecutive fourth-round exits in Toronto and Cincinnati. Rybakina had to take a brief break after she was forced to stop playing in her quarterfinal match against Iga Swiatek in Cincinnati because of a foot injury, but she was healthy in time for a tournament where she had never done particularly well, failing to advance past the fourth round until this year. “I honestly was coming here for the last 10 years, and it was never successful -- nothing close to that,” Rybakina said. “It’s just incredible. I’m falling in love with New York more and more.” Arthur Ashe Stadium, meanwhile, had been Sabalenka’s house, with four straight trips to the final and six to at least the semis. Whatever troubled her during the summer seemed forgotten once she was back in New York — until Saturday. Sabalenka repeatedly looked toward her coaches’ box with her palms up, wondering why everything was going so poorly, and showed much more frustration than that when she double-faulted to hand Rybakina a 3-2 lead in the first set. Rybakina hit the serve back and the ball bounced directly to Sabalenka, who whacked it into the crowd, earning a warning from the chair umpire. Sabalenka eventually began putting consistent pressure on Rybakina in the second set. She picked up two break points with a chance to end the set with a 5-4 lead, and though Rybakina won four straight points to get out of that jam, Sabalenka got another chance in the next service game and this time capitalized, stepping into a return to set up a miss by Rybakina.

articles.title: New world No. 1 Elena Rybakina wins maiden US Open title in three-set thriller
articles.summary: Women’s No. 2 seed Elena Rybakina will have a lot to celebrate come Monday after defeating top seed Aryna Sabalenka 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 in the US Open women’s singles final at Arthur Ashe Stadium on Saturday.
articles.body: Women’s No. 2 seed Elena Rybakina will have a lot to celebrate come Monday after defeating top seed Aryna Sabalenka 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 in the US Open women’s singles final at Arthur Ashe Stadium on Saturday. Rybakina not only won her first career title at Flushing Meadows, but will also replace Sabalenka atop the women’s tennis rankings. It only took Rybakina 44 minutes to dispatch Sabalenka 6-4 in the first set. The Belarusian Sabalenka looked at odds with herself for a good portion of the opening set, making her feelings known about the struggles as she mouthed her displeasure to herself and her coaching box. And in an even more shocking outcome, Rybakina, the Russian-born Kazakhstani, won the set while only completing only 27% of her first serves in. Despite her struggles, she only lost eight of the 30 points off her serve and never faced a break point. But like Sabalenka has done many times in her illustrious career, she battled back and looked more in control throughout the second set. The 28-year-old, while up 5-4, had the chance to put the set away twice but both times, Rybakina drew right back to tie it up at 5-5. Sabalenka was eventually able to close out the set 7-5 and force a decisive third set. The 27-year-old Rybakina came out on a mission to start the third set, quickly jumping out to a 5-2 double-break lead, putting Sabalenka on the ropes with the frustration coming back to haunt her. At match point, Rybakina served up an ace to secure the victory. As she celebrated the win, Sabalenka flung her racket to the ground before going to embrace her at the net. Following a brief hug, she sat down on the bench and smashed the same racket. The win gives Rybakina her third career grand slam, the first one since her win at the Australian Open earlier this year. Rybakina earned a reported $5.5 million, the largest prize in Grand Slam history, and tied Sabalenka and French Open winner Mirra Andreeva with a tour-high three titles this season. Rybakina said it was “tough to finds words” following the victory. “I didn’t expect nothing like this coming to this tournament,” Rybakina said. “I’ve been dealing with a little injury but somehow everything aligned together on my side.” She praised Sabalenka, calling her a “great champion.” “It’s so difficult to play against you. You push to such limits. I was dying on the court and just tried to get all the possible balls … I can’t find the words, I am sorry.” Rybakina also thanked the spectators for an “amazing atmosphere,” reflecting back on her struggles in New York previously. “I honestly was coming here for the last 10 years and it was never successful. Nothing close to that. Its just incredible. I am falling in love with New York more and more and it’s more amazing memories for me,” Rybakina added. An emotional Sabalenka thanked the New York crowd for their support over the past two weeks. “Obviously, I am disappointed but I want to congratulate Elena on an incredible year, incredible result” Sabalenka told ESPN. “Well deserved, enjoy it, have fun tonight, tomorrow, and until the end of the season so I can play well and win some titles.” With Saturday’s loss, Sabalenka’s win streak at the US Open has been snapped at 19 matches. Sabalenka had previously won this tournament in 2024 and 2025 after losing to Coco Gauff in the 2023 championship match. She could have become the third-ever woman to win three straight in the open era, joining Serena Williams and Chris Evert. This story has been updated with the latest information.

articles.title: US Open 2026 results: Elena Rybakina beats Aryna Sabalenka to win New York title
articles.summary: Elena Rybakina demonstrates why she is the best women's player in the world by beating Aryna Sabalenka to win her first US Open title.
articles.body:
Elena Rybakina demonstrated why she is the best women's player in the world by beating two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka to win her first US Open title.

Kazakhstan's Rybakina already knew she would be the new world number one after Saturday's final regardless of the result, and she celebrated with a 6-4 5-7 6-2 victory over the player she will replace.

Rybakina was the more composed of the two throughout as she claimed the third Grand Slam title of her career, having triumphed at Wimbledon in 2022 and the Australian Open earlier this year.

Sabalenka hoped to soften the blow of losing the top ranking by winning a third consecutive US Open title - but looked fraught in a tense performance.

Rybakina and Sabalenka have developed a strong rivalry built not only on their outstanding talent but their contrasting personalities.

And Rybakina's ice-cool composure - the direct opposite of the Belarusian's combustible nature - was a key difference as she took control at Flushing Meadows.

Rybakina stayed calm in an opening set where her first serve let her down and, despite her biggest weapon not firing on all cylinders, was able to execute a devastating returning game which left Sabalenka frustrated.

Sabalenka's groundstrokes improved as Rybakina's level dropped slightly in a tighter second set, taking her third opportunity to force a decider when she swarmed over Rybakina's second serve in the 12th game.

But the loose shots from Sabalenka reappeared in the third set - as did the negativity.

Rybakina's deep returning pinned Sabalenka to the baseline as she broke for a 2-1 lead, which allowed the incoming world number one to grow in stature.

There was a sign of nerves when Rybakina produced a double fault on her first championship point, but she reset admirably to hammer down an ace and underline her status as the best player in the world.

From struggling to walk to lifting trophy - how Rybakina triumphed

'Tough to control emotions' as Sabalenka suffers another near-miss

Listen to All About US Open: Rybakina crowned champion as Sabalenka melts down

Rybakina claims New York win few predicted

Rybakina rarely shows emotion on the court but there was a brief flash of a smile as she clinched her second major victory of an outstanding 2026 season.

That illustrated the sense of satisfaction she felt after winning a title few had predicted - not only because she had never previously gone beyond the last 16 in New York but the circumstances coming into the final major of the season.

With her penetrating serve and thunderous groundstrokes, Rybakina has a brand of first-strike tennis that can take the racquet out of anyone's hands.

Therefore it has been a surprise she has not enjoyed greater success on the Flushing Meadows hard courts, perhaps a result of her personality not being particularly suited to the brash nature of New York.

"I was coming here for the last 10 years and it was never successful. I'm falling in love with New York more and more," Rybakina, 27, said.

What makes the second seed's victory even more remarkable is that she was unsure if she would be fit enough to even play.

Rybakina was unable to walk for several days after injuring her ankle in the Cincinnati Open quarter-finals, putting her chances of competing here in serious jeopardy.

Not only was Rybakina able to play, but she cruised through her opening four matches thanks to a huge service game that rarely allowed opponents to get into points.

Rybakina's next two wins over China's Zheng Qinwen and home favourite Coco Gauff required more work after losing the first sets, proving she had the durability to come through tough battles.

Against Sabalenka, she showed both facets of her game, bullying her from the baseline and digging in when necessary to leave her only a French Open title away from the career Grand Slam.

"Some magic is happening. I was unlucky with injury and just going day by day," Rybakina told Sky Sports.

"We didn't know how it was going to be so I'm super happy and still can't believe it."

Emotional Sabalenka falls short in another major final

The chance to beat the woman who had taken her number one ranking was extra motivation for Sabalenka.

However, it was evident from the early stages that the stress of the situation was still troubling the four-time major singles champion - and Rybakina's superb return of serve in the early exchanges only exacerbated it.

The pressure Sabalenka was feeling manifested in some aggressive second serves, and it was unsurprising to see one go long for a double fault on the decisive break point in the opening set.

While Sabalenka showed the resilience which she has demonstrated in her ascent to the top of the sport, she never looked completely at ease.

Dramatic displays of emotion designed to let off steam - yelling, flinging her arms in the air, bouncing her racquet off the court and hiding underneath her towel - were not enough to help produce a gutsy victory which would have ranked among her best.

Instead she will have to come to terms with another near miss at a Grand Slam.

It was Sabalenka's fifth defeat from nine majors final and provides further weight to the argument that she has underachieved at the biggest tournaments given her dominance on the WTA Tour.

"The last thing I want to do right now is give a speech but I will try my best," an emotional Sabalenka told the 24,000 crowd on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

"I wish I could have performed a little bit better, but I guess next year."

articles.body:
Elena Rybakina delivered a devastating performance to dethrone two-time defending champion Aryna ⁠⁠Sabalenka with a 6-4⁠⁠, 5- 7, 6-2 win in the US Open women’s singles final, earning a third Grand Slam crown to accompany her ascent to world number one.

The ⁠⁠Russian-born Kazakh’s icy composure on the grand stage helped her snap Sabalenka’s 20-match winning streak at Flushing Meadows on Saturday, denying the Belarusian the chance to emulate Serena Williams and ⁠⁠Chris Evert with three straight New York titles.

An ankle injury had threatened to derail Rybakina’s campaign even before the tournament started, but the 27-year-old shrugged off those concerns to add the US Open title to her Australian Open triumph this year and Wimbledon success in 2022.

The ‌‌title showdown at Arthur Ashe Stadium had all the ingredients of a classic between the top two in the rankings, and though Sabalenka brought late aggression, Rybakina was typically unruffled and prevailed to pocket the $5.5m prize.

Dressed in a yellow-and-black outfit that evoked a bee, Rybakina produced some stinging groundstrokes but was unable to make the early pressure count as Sabalenka unleashed big serves to hold firm in the ⁠⁠pair’s third Grand Slam final meeting.

The second seed drew first blood ⁠⁠to go ahead 3-2 following a Sabalenka double fault, with the frustrated Belarusian earning a code violation immediately afterwards for launching a ball high into the stands of the main showcourt.

Sabalenka’s irritation became increasingly evident with ⁠⁠each missed shot and squandered opportunity, in stark contrast to the trademark calm etched on Rybakina’s face as the Kazakh tightened ⁠⁠her grip on the opening set and clinched it ⁠⁠with a tight hold.

A sudden drop-off in Rybakina’s level midway through the second set gave the 28-year-old Sabalenka hope, and she produced a delicate drop shot and a stunning backhand crosscourt winner en route to forcing a ‌‌deciding set.

Sabalenka let out a huge roar after another backhand winner to hold in a tight opening game of the third set.

However, Rybakina’s quality shone through her red-and-blue-framed racket ‌‌as ‌‌she took a commanding 5-2 lead and then closed out a famous triumph to leave her Belarusian rival without any major silverware in 2026.

Rybakina ​won ‌her ​first US Open, beating top seed ‌and defending champion ⁠Sabalenka ​6-4 ​5-7 ⁠6-2 on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

Even in the beginning we didn't know how it was going to be so I'm super happy and very proud. I still can't believe it.

"I was relieved to get to No 1 but I knew there were two more matches to push and it would be such a milestone winning the tournament here so I was focussed and trying not to see too many messages.

The title showdown on a packed Arthur Ashe Stadium had all ​the ingredients of a classic between the top two in the ⁠rankings.

Dressed in a yellow-and-black outfit that evoked a bee, Rybakina ‌produced some stinging groundstrokes but was unable to make the early pressure count as Sabalenka unleashed big serves to hold firm in the pair's third Grand Slam final ‌meeting.

The second seed drew first blood to go ahead 3-2 following a Sabalenka double fault, with the frustrated Belarusian earning a code violation immediately afterwards for launching a ball high into the stands.

A sudden drop-off in Rybakina's level midway through the second set gave the ⁠28-year-old Sabalenka hope, and she produced a stunning drop shot and a stunning backhand crosscourt winner en route to forcing a deciding set.

Sabalenka let out a huge roar after another ⁠backhand winner to hold in a tight opening ​game of the third set.

However, Rybakina's quality shone through her red-and-blue-framed racket ​as she took a commanding 5-2 lead and then closed out a famous triumph to leave her Belarusian rival without any ‌major silverware in 2026.

Sabalenka said: "The last thing I want to do right now is give a speech, but I'll try my very best. Thank you everyone. Thank you for all your support.

"I want to congratulate Elena on an incredible year, an incredible result. Well deserved. Enjoy it tonight, and have fun. So I can win some titles!

"I wish I could have performed a little bit better, but I guess there's next year."

She later spoke about smashing a ball into the crowd and breaking a racket during her press conference, saying: "It's really tough to control your emotions when you lose in the final of the Grand Slam and when you were trying to go for three-peat.

"I just wanted to let it go, because if I would hold it inside, right now or here or there on the court, I wouldn't be able to say a word or I would just go not really nice over there. I just wanted to let all of that aggression and disappointment go outside."

Navratilova: Sabalenka simply did not know what to do - she usually dominates!

"We do not see that. Usually it's Sabalenka doing the bullying.

"I think that's why Sabalenka didn't know what to do. She's used to dictating, to putting people on the defence, on their heels and rushing shots.

"Instead, it was all Rybakina doing that to her. And I did not expect that.

"It's not that Sabalenka lost the match, Rybakina won it. She earned that win.

"It will be back to the drawing board for Sabalenka. What will she do next time if Rybakina is playing this well?"

Bartoli: Extraordinary Rybakina can do anything on a tennis court

"Can you imagine that her previous best result here was the fourth round?

"That's extraordinary, to come here with all the pressure of the world, knowing she had the No 1 world ranking on her racket, to actually go on and win the title.

"The way she bounced back at the beginning of the third set tonight for me, was absolutely extraordinary.

"It looked like she completely forgot what happened at the backend of that second set, when she got caught on her own service game.

"She just kept on moving on, and moving forward all the time. The way she attacked Sabalenka's serve all the time, putting her under so much pressure.

"The ball-striking from that young lady is just something else. She can do anything on the tennis court.

"She's only missing Roland Garros now from completing a career Grand Slam."

Robson: Key difference was Rybakina's lights out backhand

"We were excited about this final for good reason. Because of how well we know both of these players perform on big occasions like this.

"For Rybakina, without even crowd support on her side, she just did not flinch.

"Yes, you could maybe point to the double faults at the end, but under so much pressure, and Sabalenka trying everything to make a comeback in that third set, she just kept going for her shots.

"It is just unbelievable how hard both of these players hit the ball. Their timing is phenomenal.

"The difference today was the backhand from Rybakina, which was lights out from start to finish."

articles.title: The New Queen of New York: Elena Rybakina's US Open win cranks up tennis' next great rivalry
articles.summary: Rybakina has taken over Aryna Sabalenka's spot atop the women's tennis world in more ways than one.
articles.body:
NEW YORK — Aryna Sabalenka rolled into New York two weeks ago as the No. 1 player in the world and the two-time defending US Open champion. Over the course of those two weeks, leading up to Saturday's final, Elena Rybakina claimed Sabalenka's No. 1 ranking, halted her US Open run, and reduced her to a seething, racket-smashing fury. Not bad for a fortnight's work, not bad for another chapter in what's developing into the finest rivalry in women's tennis.

Sabalenka and Rybakina are the two finest players in women's tennis right now, and their US Open final match — which ended with a 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 Rybakina victory — was always going to be a heavyweight fight, strength on strength. But over the course of three sets, Rybakina turned Sabalenka's greatest asset — her furious willpower — against her, hemming Sabalenka in on all sides and, by the end of the match, smothering all hope.

"I feel like the match itself was so close, and even first set, I got an early break and then it was kind of a little bit easier to step in, to be aggressive," Rybakina said afterward. "And then in the second … I feel like she just played in these important moments more aggressive, and she just went for the shots. I had some little opportunities, made a couple of mistakes. But then in the third set, I told myself that I can still do it. I need to focus on my serve and just risk a little bit more when I have the chance."

No point better exemplified this match than the one at 15-15 in the fourth game of the final set. Already up a break, Rybakina simply gave Sabalenka nowhere to run, no chance for escape, mixing deep volleys and drop shots until Sabalenka ran herself right out of the point — and, a few games later, right out of the match.

Rybakina didn't overwhelm Sabalenka with dominant tennis. She didn't wow the crowd at Arthur Ashe Stadium with artistic tennis. She simply played relentless tennis — minimizing her own mistakes, taking advantage of Sabalenka's many errors, and never letting the match get too far out of her control. That's how you win a major, that's how you build the foundation for an epic career … and that's how you get the Arthur Ashe Stadium crowd on your side, too.

"I honestly was coming here for the last 10 years and it was never successful," Rybakina said immediately after the match. "Nothing close to that. It's just incredible. I'm falling in love with New York more and more. It's an amazing memory for me." Absent star power or American citizenship, US Open crowds tend to cheer for whoever's performing well in a given match, and although Sabalenka clearly had their favor early on, Rybakina won them over by the end of the third set.

Every match hinges on which player will exploit the narrow margins that lead to victory or defeat, and time and time again on Saturday, Rybakina kept the match close enough to the point where she could exploit those margins. The two were tied at 71 points apiece heading into the final set; Rybakina ended up with 103 points to Sabalenka's 90. Sabalenka landed more of her first serves — 58 percent to Rybakina's 47 percent — but Rybakina converted many more of those first serves to points, 85 percent to 69 percent.

One more number that's crucial for the emotional flow of the match: Rybakina had 24 unforced errors to Sabalenka's 35. Those misfires caused Sabalenka to doubt herself, to rage at herself and her coaching staff, to lose control on multiple occasions. After surrendering what turned out to be a decisive break in the fifth game of the first set, Sabalenka angrily slapped a ball into the crowd. That earned her a warning from the chair during the changeover. And after the final point, Sabalenka smashed her racket on the court, then continued hammering away with it when she sat down on her bench.

"It's really tough to control your emotions when you're in the final of the Grand Slam and when you were trying to go for three-peat," a calmer — but in no way apologetic — Sabalenka explained afterward. "So I just wanted to let it go because if I would hold it inside … I wouldn't be able to say a word or I would just go not really nice [on the court]. So I just wanted all of that aggression and disappointment to go outside."

Tennis is always at its best when there's a rivalry at the very top of the pyramid — think Chris Evert vs. Martina Navratilova or Steffi Graf vs. Monica Seles. Sabalenka vs. Rybakina — Aryna vs. Elena, if you like — has the potential to reach that level, particularly if Sabalenka can capitalize on the momentum of her US Open run next season.

"It's always very difficult matches against Aryna, and I feel like we push each other to be better after such tough battles," Rybakina said. "You always want to try something new, to change in your game to be better, and I don't know what the future is going to bring, but I hope success and some more wins."

Sabalenka still leads the head-to-head match 10-8. And of the 11 matches that have gone three sets, Sabalenka has won eight of them. But Rybakina has now knocked off Sabalenka in two Grand Slam finals this year — the US and Australian Opens — and judging from Sabalenka's post-match expression, it's safe to say that Rybakina has firmly taken up residence in her head.

So Sabalenka's reign ends, and Rybakina's begins. Sabalenka held the No. 1 title for 99 weeks.

"Well, that's amazing," Sabalenka said, when told of that number, and swelled a bit with pride. "Let's see if Elena can beat me in that." Then she remembered what had just happened, and walked it back a couple steps.

"If she continues playing like that," Sabalenka said, "then I'm in trouble."

I’ve been dealing with a little bit with an injury, but somehow everything aligned together on my side.”The triumph also completed a remarkable hard-court double for Rybakina, who defeated Sabalenka in the Australian Open final earlier this year. She now needs only the French Open title to complete a career Grand Slam, having already won Wimbledon in 2022.Rybakina keeps her cool as Sabalenka faltersThe final had all the ingredients of another classic between the world's top two players, but Rybakina's trademark composure ultimately proved decisive.The second seed immediately put pressure on Sabalenka's serve and created 12 break opportunities, converting three. Rybakina, the WTA Tour's leading ace hitter, struggled to find her usual rhythm on first serve, landing less than half of them in play, but compensated with relentless returning and clean ball-striking.Sabalenka's frustration surfaced early. After double-faulting to hand Rybakina a 3-2 lead in the opening set, she smashed a ball into the stands and received a code violation. Rybakina then held her nerve to take the first set 6-4.Sabalenka responded in the second, raising her aggression and finally finding a way through Rybakina's defences. After the Kazakh saved two break points while serving at 4-4, Sabalenka created another opportunity in the next game and this time converted it to level the match.But Rybakina regained control in the deciding set. Despite showing a rare flash of frustration after missing a backhand on break point in the opening game, she quickly settled again and surged ahead 5-2 before closing out the biggest victory of her career in New York.Sabalenka, who had been chasing a third consecutive US Open title, could only watch the opportunity disappear.“I was just out there competing, trying to do my best with what I had there today,” Sabalenka said after the match. “Not good enough.”Sabalenka's New York reign endsThe defeat ended Sabalenka's 19-match winning streak at the US Open and denied her a place alongside Serena Williams and Chris Evert as a three-time consecutive champion in New York.Sabalenka had dominated Arthur Ashe Stadium in recent years, reaching four straight US Open finals and at least the semifinals in six consecutive appearances. But Rybakina's combination of power, accuracy and remarkable calm proved too much.Sabalenka herself acknowledged the danger posed by her opponent.“Her serve is amazing, the way she's able to step in and overpower you on court, and especially if it’s a U.S. Open court where it’s super fast, it's definitely a huge advantage for her,” Sabalenka said. “A lot of things make her dangerous.”The result also flipped the rankings at the top of women's tennis. Sabalenka had occupied No. 1 for 99 consecutive weeks, but Rybakina will officially take over the position on Monday.For Rybakina, however, the biggest prize was the one she lifted at the end of the night. She earned $5.5 million — the largest prize in Grand Slam history — and turned a tournament that had once been a source of frustration into the scene of her greatest New York triumph.“I honestly was coming here for the last 10 years, and it was never successful -- nothing close to that,” Rybakina said. “It’s just incredible. I’m falling in love with New York more and more.”Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.summary: Elena Rybakina arrived in New York unable to walk without pain after injuring her foot. She leaves the city as the US Open champion and new world number one.
articles.body:
Elena Rybakina arrived in New York unable to walk without pain after injuring her foot. She leaves the city as the US Open champion and new world number one.

Kazakhstan's Rybakina produced a brilliant performance to beat two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka 6-4 5-7 6-2 in Saturday's final and repeat her Australian Open success against the same player in January.

Clutching the trophy on Saturday night, Rybakina reflected that "some magic is happening" for her after her difficult lead-in to the tournament.

The 27-year-old aggravated a foot injury during her quarter-final in Cincinnati against Iga Swiatek last month, a little over a week before the final major of the year began.

Playing on through injury could have had dire consequences for the rest of her season - but Rybakina, knowing the top ranking was in her grasp, wanted to try and play in the final Grand Slam of the year.

"I was so upset. I didn't know actually how it was going to be day by day," she said.

"We arrived in New York and did an MRI. It didn't look that great.

"I couldn't even walk for the next few days without pain.

"I was lucky enough to have a very good doctor in Australia. She was on the phone with us all the time and somehow, with the team, we made a plan."

Rybakina did not do any on-court training for a week, but daily recovery sessions in the gym - plus trips for dinner and to the cinema to "switch the mind" - helped get her ready for another major triumph.

She won her first four matches at Flushing Meadows without dropping a set, including seeing off four-time major winner Naomi Osaka.

Her run from then on - which included beating Olympic champion Zheng Qinwen in the quarter-finals, outlasting third seed Coco Gauff in the semis and outplaying top seed Sabalenka in the final - was nothing short of outstanding.

"I was so unlucky with the injury, but I'm very proud," Rybakina said.

'Tough to control emotions' as Sabalenka suffers another near-miss

Rybakina wins US Open to inflict further pain on Sabalenka

Listen: US Open podcast - Rybakina crowned champion

Rybakina had already been confirmed as world number one by reaching the semi-finals in New York. The fact that her final opponent was Sabalenka, the player she will replace at the top of the rankings, added an extra dimension to Saturday's championship match.

Rybakina won the first set despite her serve, one of her biggest weapons, misfiring.

She landed only 27% of her first serves during the opener, but still won 22 of 30 points behind her serve and did not face a break point as she took the lead.

Sabalenka eventually broke in the 12th game of the second set to send their match the distance, but it was Rybakina who dominated the decider.

While her Belarusian opponent grew visibly more frustrated as the final slipped away, Rybakina remained remarkably composed.

"The way she [Rybakina] quietly walks around, she doesn't really lift her head up and she gives no emotion away whatsoever," former British number one Annabel Croft said on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"Rybakina is like a machine out there. You never know what's going on in her head."

However, nerves did show when Rybakina threw in two double faults as she served for the title.

At 40-30, the trophy in her sights, Rybakina could have blinked. Instead, she coolly sent down her 12th ace of the match to secure her third Grand Slam title.

The second seed produced her biggest celebration of her three major wins - a smile and both arms raised in celebration as she took in the applause.

Rybakina has now won two of her three Grand Slam finals against Sabalenka, all of which have come on their favoured hard courts.

On Monday, Rybakina will become the 30th different women to top the world rankings.

She is a different personality to Sabalenka, who held the position for the past 99 weeks, but Croft believes she will "take it in her stride".

"I actually think she has the right personality to deal with it," Croft said.

"There are going to be a lot of players around her nipping at her heels. She can fluctuate with her levels, but when it really matters, we've seen her be able to bring it to the table.

"It's not going to be easy to hang on to it. I think women's tennis is really exciting right now."

Rybakina has completed three parts of the career Grand Slam, with just a French Open victory missing from her collection.

After winning Wimbledon in 2022, she did not claim her second major until January's Australian Open, and has now added a third in New York.

She has never previously been further than the quarter-finals at Roland Garros, although she did win a WTA 1,000 event on clay in Rome in 2023.

Former British number one Laura Robson said on Sky Sports: "She is an all-surface player - clay is the worst one, but when you get her on something that's quite lively or quick, she's unplayable at times.

"I genuinely think she will win many more Slams. I just don't see, when her serve and return are on, how pretty much anyone can beat her on a hard court."

articles.title: US Open 2026 results: How Aryna Sabalenka emotions encapsulated season of setbacks
articles.summary: After losing another Grand Slam final, Aryna Sabalenka smashes her racquet in frustration at a year that has seen her lose her world number one status.
articles.body:
Aryna Sabalenka cut a forlorn figure as she sat staring into space following a painful defeat by Elena Rybakina in the US Open final.

As Rybakina celebrated her third Grand Slam title following a 6-4 5-7 6-2 win in New York, cameras pictured Sabalenka deep in thought as she sat in silence with her team.

At a tournament which has delivered so much success for two-time champion Sabalenka, the disappointment the 28-year-old has faced in the past week leaves her with plenty to ponder.

Not only has Rybakina replaced Sabalenka as the world number one after 99 weeks at the summit, she has now ended the Belarusian's 20-match winning streak at Flushing Meadows.

Defeat also means Sabalenka will end the year without winning a Grand Slam title for the first time since 2022.

For four-time Grand Slam singles champion Sabalenka, the disappointment was palpable.

Throughout the final, faced with a composed Rybakina who put together an outstanding performance, Sabalenka could not keep her frustrations at bay.

Her racquet felt the brunt of her exasperation as she slammed it to the ground after offering a break point to Rybakina in the second set.

After Rybakina sent an ace past her to secure victory, Sabalenka flung her racquet away in disgust before congratulating her opponent. As Rybakina waved to the crowd, Sabalenka sat on her chair and smashed another racquet against the floor.

Sabalenka also used an expletive as she told a cameraperson to go away as she sat with her team immediately after defeat.

"It's really tough to control your emotions when you lose in the final of the Grand Slam and when you were trying to go for three-peat," Sabalenka said afterwards.

"So I just wanted to let it go, because if I would hold it inside, right now or here or there on the court, I wouldn't be able to say a word or I would just go not really nice over there.

"So I just wanted to let all of that aggression and disappointment go outside."

Rybakina wins US Open to inflict further pain on Sabalenka

From struggling to walk to lifting trophy - how Rybakina triumphed

Sabalenka is always vocal on court and has been known to berate herself and roll her eyes ironically when missing points, even in her most dominant of victories.

Often she can channel her emotions into her aggressive hitting, but former British number one Annabel Croft believes it contributed to her downfall against Rybakina.

"It was extraordinary to witness because she had been very negative on herself with her body language in that first set and suddenly the emotions got the better of her," Croft said on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"I felt like that really contributed to her going down in that first set. She was beating herself."

Sabalenka held back tears during a post-match interview in which she praised Rybakina's performance.

Croft says the Belarusian would benefit from applying the same level of poise during her matches.

"I think what happened was the minute she started to not respect the level of tennis her opponent was playing, she couldn't handle it at all," said Croft.

"You have to respect what they're putting out there and applaud it but then find ways to dig in and find another way to compete with them.

"It was almost like throwing the toys out of the pram today."

The weight of expectation Sabalenka puts on herself has affected her in major finals in particular.

She has won four of her nine Grand Slam singles finals, and only won one of her four finals as the world number one.

All five of her major final losses were in three sets, and on two of those occasions Sabalenka won the opening set.

After defending her US Open crown in 2025, she began this year targeting more Grand Slam success.

However, she lost a tight three-set Australian Open final to Rybakina before she imploded at the French Open. Leading Russia's Diana Shnaider by a set and 4-1 in the quarter-finals, Sabalenka totally lost her way, being dragged into a decider that she lost 6-0.

At Wimbledon, Sabalenka lost in the fourth round to Japanese four-time Grand Slam winner Naomi Osaka in what was her earliest Grand Slam exit for four years.

Sabalenka has won three WTA titles this year, triumphing in Brisbane, Indian Wells and the Miami Open, but she has been second best to Rybakina in the hard-court majors.

The US Open was meant to salvage Sabalenka's season - but she must now regroup as she adjusts to her position as world number two.

"I think overall I should be happy with the level I played, and there's lots of things to take from this tournament," Sabalenka said.

"Experience shows that I only come back stronger and all of these lessons this season definitely already made me stronger, but definitely going to motivate me for the next year to do a better job."

articles.title: The US Open did what Grand Slams Should: Showed us who’s best
articles.summary: Saturday’s US Open women’s singles final provided a clear and convincing answer to the question - “Who is the best woman on the planet?”
articles.body: We say that sports are about everything and anything: community, identity, fitting in and standing out. Sports are political, cultural, artistic and often deeply personal. Those stories — narrative or allegorical — are in specifics or else in the context. They manifest through sports, but not without the prism of other factors. In truth, though, what sports are actually about — all of them, always, when stripped down to the essence — is figuring out who is better than whom. And, ultimately, who is the best. It would get boring if it was only ever that. But sometimes the straightforward pursuit of hierarchy is enough. No history at stake, no Americans for the hometown crowd to latch onto. When the players were introduced for the women’s final of the US Open, the crowd swelled as it was explained that first up was the woman who would assume the top ranking in the world come Monday. The emcee didn’t make this part explicit, but her opponent Saturday afternoon was the same woman she’ll replace in that spot. Aryna Sabalenka entered the tournament ranked No. 1 in the world. She entered Saturday the two-time reigning women’s singles US Open champion. Isn’t it just perfectly neat and tidy then that Elena Rybakina, who will replace her as the former — a fact already sealed by virtue of her performance prior to the final — also took her crown for the latter? In a clash of comparable strength and contrasting styles, Rybakina beat Sabalenka 6-4, 5-7, 6-2. “This game is very simple and very binary,” Martin Blackman, who spent a decade as the general manager of USTA Player Development, told CNN Sports this week. “If I’m ranked 19 and you’re ranked 18, you’re better than me, until I beat you.” Or, as it was on Saturday, No. 2 and No. 1. Out of four billion women alive on planet earth right now, someone is the singular best at the sport of tennis. You could credibly claim that on Saturday in Queens, New York, we found her. How’s that for the stakes to make a compelling story? No fluffy stuff, no soft focus. Just a cold-blooded clash of elite athletes with a clear winner and a clear loser. Especially early in the match, it was so quiet in the stadium that you could hear how quiet Rybakina was. Every volley created a consistent rhythm: a reverberating “Eeyugh!” from Sabalenka followed by a beat of silence. In the first set, Sabalenka seemed caught off guard by an opponent who could not only match her power but best it. At 6-foot, Sabalenka is tall; Rybakina is ever so slightly taller. Sabalenka serves hard and fast; but Rybakina serves faster. When Rybakina broke Sabalenka’s serve to take a 3-2 lead in the opening set, the outgoing No. 1 responded by earning a code violation from the umpire by smacking a ball into the stands. When she clinched the first set of the match that would make her a champion, Rybakina celebrated with a subdued fist pump. If she made a sound the entire match, it wasn’t louder than the squeak of her sneakers. See, there I go - extrapolating the simple into something bigger. Poise versus pugnacity. But Sabalenka didn’t lose because she competed in 127 carats of ostentatious custom jewelry worth $400,000. She has succeeded plenty while refusing to temper her, well, temper or anything else about her fierce and demonstrative personality. This was her fourth-straight US Open Finals appearance, and her first loss since she fell to Coco Gauff on the same stage in 2023. She lost because Rybakina was better. For the final point of the women’s tournament, Rybakina froze her rival with a perfect serve. Sabalenka barely budged from her defensive crouch. There was nothing she could do but watch her grip on the top spot in the sport bounce away blithely. In the immediate aftermath, she threw her racquet to the ground, retrieved it, and hugged her defeater mutely, before retreating to her bench where the racquet took a beating that bent it out of shape. Meanwhile, the woman who won did very little worth noting. “I wish I could perform a little bit better,” Sabalenka said as part of the on-court ceremony after the match. She seemed close to tears. “But I guess next year,” she concluded, her confidence overcoming the disappointment. By contrast, Rybakina – who, again, had already clinched the top rank in the world – seemed stunned by her own success: “I didn’t expect nothing like this coming to this tournament,” she said as pyrotechnics waited behind to erupt in fiery fanfare befitting her serve far more than her soft-spoken persona. “It’s so difficult to play against you,” Rybakina continued, addressing her opponent directly during the post-match ceremony. Difficult, but not impossible. After all, she started her rise to No. 1 by opening the season with a win at the Australian Open over Sabalenka. Later, in a press conference with media members, Rybakina offered an anodyne review of the rivalry. “I feel like we push each other to be better,” she said of Sabalenka. Probably she didn’t know then that her rival had already thrown down another gauntlet. Earlier, Sabalenka had said of her own run atop the rankings, “I think it’s an incredible achievement, and I don’t even know how many weeks I was able to be there.” Someone else in the room supplied the answer. “99 [weeks]? Well, that’s amazing,” Sabalenka said. “Let’s see if Elena can beat me in that.”

articles.body:
The viral "Burgundy Prophecy" is alive and well at the US Open.

World No. 1 Elena Rybakina wore an all-burgundy outfit while arriving at Arthur Ashe Stadium for her US Open final against Aryna Sabalenka on Saturday.

The outfit worked wonders as the Kazakh beat the two-time reigning champion 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 to claim her third career major title and first-ever title at Flushing Meadows.

After Rybakina's win, the US Open X account made sure to highlight that the good fortune that accompanies burgundy is real. Tennis fans will remember that the winners of the last two men's titles — Jannik Sinner (2024) and Carlos Alcaraz (2025) — both wore burgundy kits during their respective wins, following the tradition of several other former champions in New York. Spanish legend Rafael Nadal also wore a burgundy kit during his 2022 US Open win.

Even more eerily, Czech duo Karolina Muchova and Jakub Mensik wore matching burgundy outfits en route their US Open Mixed Doubles title late last month.

While Rybakina didn't wear a burgundy kit on the court, the pre-match fit was enough to complete the prophecy.

American World No. 1 Jessica Pegula wore a burgundy kit during her 2026 US Open run but fell to Sabalenka in the semifinal. But during her run, several fans credited her kit for her outstanding play that nearly helped her win her first major title.

With her win, Rybakina joined former World No. 1s Iga Swiatek (six) and Sabalenka (four) as the only woman to win three or more major titles since the start of the decade. The Kazakh has now won one Wimbledon (2022), one Australian Open (2026) and a US Open (2026) title, furthering her reputation as one of the best players of her era.

She also became just the second player since Steffi Graff (1995) to beat the World No. 1 in multiple Grand Slam finals in the same calendar year, following her win over Sabalenka in the Australian Open final at the start of the year.

Rybakina thanked the Belarusian for pushing her to her limit.

"I just want to say Aryna you're a great champion," she said at the podium after her win.

"It's so difficult to play you. You push to such a limit. I was doubting on the court and trying to get to all the possible balls. Congrats to you for all the achievements. Congrats to your team. You guys are doing an amazing job. I can't find the words now, sorry.

"I was coming here for the last ten years and was never successful. Nothing close to that. It's just incredible. I'm falling in love with New York more and more. It's amazing memories for me. Thank you guys."
